prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation, in which designed small molecules bring ubiquitin ligases and chosen proteins together to destroy them catalytically

statement.case_for: I keep targeted protein degradation as a single-part prize for Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli. The round-1 exchange confirmed that it is the only configuration on which five members converge in topic, and every member who discussed it described the same scientific core: event-driven, catalytic destruction through induced proximity replaces occupancy-based pharmacology. That is a molecular-design principle, and it is supported by a real physical-chemistry base in ternary-complex cooperativity, linker design and VHL ligand structure. Crews and Deshaies conceived and first demonstrated the concept in 2001, and Ciulli's structure-guided work turned it from a proof of concept into a design discipline that other laboratories could reproduce and extend. The mechanism is independently confirmed and clinical-stage degraders are numerous, so the scientific case does not depend on a future approval. After weighing the chair's questions, I judge that the competing single-topic configurations (perovskites, molecular sieves, C-N coupling with KRAS) each have a clearer attribution but a narrower base of support and, in my reading, a less original chemical principle.
statement.case_against: No degrader has been approved, so the clinical payoff is prospective, and the Committee could reasonably prefer to wait. The attribution is the harder problem and I have not resolved it. Whichever third name is chosen, a strong claim is left out: Handa and Ito for cereblon, or Ciulli for structure-guided design. A PROTAC-only citation understates the thalidomide and glue strand, which is the part currently attached to approved drugs. A citation broad enough to cover both strands is not cleanly carried by three names. A prize on this topic is therefore defensible on science but exposed to criticism on credit.

responses.point: Chabes now puts degradation first and proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa with a citation that also covers the thalidomide molecular-glue mechanism, while calling the work possibly somewhat early.
responses.response: I take the glue argument seriously, and it is the main reason I did not close the question quickly. Cereblon is the most concrete route by which degraders reach patients today. My difficulty is that a citation widened to cover glues needs more than one name from that strand: Handa and Ito identified cereblon, and the later mechanistic work on neosubstrate degradation is a separate set of contributions. Three names cannot carry both strands without dropping someone with a claim as strong as Ciulli's. I would prefer the narrower, cleaner citation on induced-proximity design, and I accept that the choice of the third name is a judgement about what the prize is for and not a finding from the record. On maturity we are close: I weigh the absence of an approved PROTAC as a timing risk and not as a defect in the discovery.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers perovskite solar absorbers (Miyasaka, Park, Snaith) as a single part and, in his degradation alternative, replaces Ciulli with Handa because cereblon underlies the approved drugs. He concedes that credit for B005 is spread beyond three people and that stability and toxicity are unresolved.
responses.response: The perovskite case is clearly chemical and the pace of independent certification is impressive. I still rank it below B020 for two reasons that he himself raises. First, Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis have claims that a trio leaves out, so the attribution problem is of the same size as in degradation but without the breadth of support. Second, the open questions on long-term stability and lead make the maturity of the technology at least as uncertain as the clinical question for degraders, and in perovskites the uncertainty bears on the same device that the prize would celebrate. On Handa, my view has not changed from round 1: his result identified the target of an existing drug and did not by itself give chemists a design rule. I would accept Handa as the third name only if the Committee deliberately decides the citation should cover glues, and then I would ask that Ciulli's omission be stated openly.

responses.point: Sparr proposes a two-part prize: Cullis alone for ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B049), and Crews and Deshaies for the PROTAC concept. She argues the two are distinct achievements and that the 2023 Medicine prize covered nucleoside modification and not the carrier.
responses.response: Her argument that lipid design is chemistry in the strict sense, through pKa tuning and non-bilayer phase behaviour, is persuasive to me, and I moved B049 from a vague alternative to a serious one. I do not support the pairing, for two reasons. First, her own file says that Cullis alone understates a team including Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and that decisive optimisation took place in companies, so the attribution for B049 is the least settled on the shortlist. Second, restricting B020 to Crews and Deshaies drops the structure-guided strand that I think makes the prize a chemistry prize and not a pharmacology one. A single part with three names on B020 keeps the credit more defensible than two parts with one name and two names that each carry a visible gap. I would keep B049 as my alternative if the Committee wants a second topic.

responses.point: The chair ranks B020 first with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, says he cannot dismiss the Handa argument, and keeps B014 as an alternative with a two-person Balasubramanian and Klenerman core.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration and I do not see a reason to complicate it. On his two-person sequencing core, I still think the cleanness of that attribution is partly produced by setting Rothberg and the pyrosequencing route aside, and that choice would be contested whichever way it is made. I therefore keep B014 as an alternative and not as my lead. If the Committee votes down the Ciulli third name, I would prefer the choice be made explicitly on the glue question, not by drifting toward Handa because he appears in two other trios.

uncertainties: Whether the third name should be Ciulli or Handa, which is a judgement about whether the citation covers glues
Whether the absence of an approved degrader should delay recognition
Whether a narrow PROTAC citation will be seen as understating the field once Handa, Ito, Sakamoto, Kim and Gray are excluded
Whether the Committee will treat sequencing or lipid nanoparticles as chemistry strongly enough to displace B020 at the vote
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict. My work on designed peptides, peptide-nanoparticle hybrids and biosensors is adjacent to some shortlisted topics (lipid nanoparticles, sequencing), but I have no collaboration with any credited name. My postdoc mentor Molly Stevens is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. This is unchanged from round 1.
